title: Broccoli AI Raises $52 Mn Across Series A And B From Khosla
summary: Broccoli AI raises 52 million dollars across Series A and B funding from Khosla Ventures
detailed: San Francisco-based startup Broccoli AI raised $52 million across Series A and Series B rounds led by Khosla Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator and Operator Partners.
The company builds AI agents for home-service businesses like plumbers, electricians, and HVAC contractors to handle customer calls, appointment booking, and estimates.

Broccoli's platform is used by over 1,500 businesses, handling more than 10 million conversations and booking 2.5 million appointments while integrating with tools like ServiceTitan and Housecall Pro.
Founder AJ Jain reported that revenue tripled since the Series A while headcount grew from 15 to over 150 employees, with the AI handling about 80% of routine office tasks.
sentences: Broccoli AI, a San Francisco-based startup founded by BITS Pilani alumni AJ Jain and Aditya Ketkar, has raised $52 million across its Series A and Series B rounds.
Khosla Ventures led both rounds, which were completed nine months apart.
Y Combinator and Operator Partners participated in both.
The company builds AI agents for plumbers, electricians and other home-service businesses.
Before this, it had raised $1.5 million in seed funding after going through Y Combinator.
The new money will go into hiring and expanding its AI across the customer journey.
Broccoli’s agents answer customer calls, book appointments, follow up on estimates, renew service memberships and re-engage past customers.
That is the office work of a contracting business, not the trade itself.

The Broccoli platform integrates with software contractors already use, including ServiceTitan, Salesforce and Housecall Pro.
That matters more than it sounds, because a tool that does not talk to the dispatch system creates work instead of removing it.
Broccoli says more than 1,500 home-service businesses use its platform.
Its agents have handled over 10 million customer conversations and booked 2.5 million service and sales appointments.
AJ Jain told Fortune that revenue has tripled since the Series A.
Headcount has grown from 15 people a year ago to more than 150.
Tripling revenue while adding 135 people is not obviously efficient.
It is, however, what a company scaling a service-heavy AI product looks like.
The company also says its AI does work equivalent to roughly 30% of a typical contractor’s office staff.
Jain’s own description is more useful than the marketing.
He says the system handles about 80% of tasks well, and the remaining 20% still needs human judgement.
Emergency calls, such as a flooded basement or a fire, get passed to people at the contractor’s office.
That is the right design choice: an AI agent that mishandles a burst pipe loses a customer permanently.
The 80% figure is also the ceiling to watch for Broccoli.
If the last 20% never comes down, Broccoli stays a very good answering service.
It does not become the operating system for a contracting business.
Samir Kaul, founding general partner at Khosla Ventures, framed the thesis around labour shortage.
Plumbers, electricians and HVAC technicians are scarce, and the ones working spend their nights on paperwork.
That is a real constraint in the United States, where skilled-trade hiring has lagged demand for a decade.
Software that absorbs administrative work lets a contractor take more jobs with the same crew.
That is a return a buyer can calculate before signing.
Backing two rounds nine months apart is also a statement about pace.
A fund that leads twice is usually watching retention and expansion revenue, not just growth.
Three things will decide whether Broccoli AI becomes infrastructure for home services or a point tool.
The first is churn among small contractors.
A 1,500-customer base in a fragmenting industry can hide a lot of turnover.
The second is pricing power per seat.
If the product replaces 30% of an office team, it should be priced against that salary.
Priced per conversation instead, it stays a small line item.
The third is the integration depth with ServiceTitan and Housecall Pro.
The deeper it sits in dispatch and billing, the harder it becomes to remove.
